text: An affair, and then a matching one: the arithmetic looks simple until two people have to live inside it. Robert Z. Leonard has 83 minutes, barely enough room for a marriage to break and then be examined, and the compression keeps the film from settling into a study of anything. What it does instead is hold a symmetry steady long enough to become uncomfortable, a wife choosing the same conduct her husband chose, in a 1929 American picture that treats the choice as a decision rather than a fall. Academy notice reached it in three places, Best Actress among them, and that is where the weight sits. The design needs a performer who can play contempt and appetite in the same look, and hold the room while the men in it recalculate.

A German officer is shot in a Dutch street in the last months of the war, and he falls in front of one house rather than the one beside it. Everything after proceeds from those few metres. Fons Rademakers gives the accident of address its full weight - who was inside, who came out, what the neighbours did - and then follows the boy who watched, across the decades in which a country settled on a story about itself. The men from the resistance are not villains here, and not quite heroes either; the film keeps returning them to him at intervals, as ordinary citizens of a peace built on top of what they did. It took the Academy's international feature award, and at 144 minutes it moves at the speed of a life rather than a case, which is the only speed at which its subject makes sense.

Eva Lovelace talks: constantly, hopefully, to whoever is standing in the room. Seventy-four minutes is all Lowell Sherman takes to move her through the New York theatre, and the economy shows in the design. Three men are arranged around her - a paternal actor, a producer whose attention wanders, a playwright who means what he says - and between them they cover most of what the profession had on offer to a young woman in 1932. The Academy's Best Actress citation is the fact the film still rests on, and the role explains why: it demands someone who can make relentless hope legible as technique rather than charm. What lasts is not the ambition plot but the sound of a person auditioning when nobody has asked her to.

Two searches run on the same track here: the woman Niccolò wants, and the woman he needs to cast. He is a film director, recently left by his wife, and the picture is unsparing about how easily those two pursuits become one activity in a man who has never had to separate them. Michelangelo Antonioni allows him 128 minutes and very little cover. The affair gets less attention than the intervals around it - the waiting, the driving, the stretches in which nothing resolves and nobody arrives - because the intervals are where the habit shows. Shot in Italian, produced out of France, it is finally about a professional way of looking that has quietly eaten the life it was meant to serve, and about a man who would call that work.

The boy wants into the business his father spent years getting out of. Francesco Munzi builds Anime Nere on that reversal - the young pushing toward the trade, the old holding a line in the Calabrian hills, where the family's money was always going to be somebody's inheritance - and he films it without the swagger the genre usually issues as standard. It took the David di Donatello for both best film and direction. At 103 minutes it is unhurried and mostly quiet, more interested in what gets said at a table than in what happens on a road, and its real subject is obligation rather than crime: nobody in it chooses to be a criminal, and nobody is offered a way to decline a debt they were born already holding.

The cruelty of it is administrative: papers signed, a family selected, and a woman left to arrange a life close enough to watch a child who will call her something else. Mitchell Leisen takes 122 minutes, long for a melodrama and right for a story whose real subject is duration - what it costs to keep one fact back, daily, at the scale of decades. It starts in the First World War with a small-town girl and a pilot passing through, and it is clear-eyed about the machinery that converts a private circumstance into a permanent civic arrangement. The Academy honoured the lead performance and the story. The performance has the harder assignment: it has to age across the film, and hold something in reserve in every scene.

Gaetano is not leaving Naples because he has to; nothing is forcing him out. He has work, he has friends, and he goes anyway, wanting different days and different people, and the comedy in Massimo Troisi's film comes from how badly the world handles a young man whose reason for departing is that unemphatic. A premise built on a refusal is difficult to make funny. What carries it is register: conversational, digressive, built out of hesitation rather than punchlines, and at 107 minutes willing to take the time a long conversation takes. Made in Italy in 1980, it is a departure story that declines the usual reason for departing, and what it wants is small and hard to say out loud - permission to begin again without a catastrophe to justify it.

Nursing school was the plan; the road that opened instead ran toward a ballot. That swerve is the comic engine, and it marks what an American picture of 1947 was willing to grant a young woman - mobility, provided it arrives by accident rather than by design. H. C. Potter plays the accident straight. Ninety-seven minutes, briskly turned, with politics presented as a house she walks into without knowing which of the doors are meant for her, and with the plainness of the outsider doing the work satire would otherwise have to do. Academy notice went to a leading and a supporting performance both, which is the correct reading of the thing: a comedy of manners needs a target secure enough to be teased, and someone to do the teasing.

He wins the acquittal, and then the acquitted man turns up beside his daughter. The logic is unpleasant and exact: a defence lawyer's professional triumph delivered to his own door, where the argument he made in court, that a charge proves nothing, is the one argument he now refuses to hear. Clarence Brown works it out in 93 minutes and lets the drinking do the rest; the father is already an alcoholic when the trouble starts, which spares the film any tidy line of cause and effect. Three Academy citations came of it, for the two leads and the direction, and the acting is where the temperature lives - a daughter who will not be governed, and a man discovering that she learned the argument from him.

Selling music contracts door to door requires a personality Sergio Benvenuti does not have. Carlo Verdone is honest about how that looks from outside: not endearing, just a man in a doorway losing. The scale stays domestic - offices, apartments, the particular humiliation of a job in which the product is the salesman's own manner - and Rome in 1981 is a place of small transactions rather than a backdrop. Help arrives from someone named Nadia, and the comedy narrows to what a shy man will agree to become in order to keep working. It took the David di Donatello for best film and for direction, a lot of official regard for a picture built entirely out of embarrassment. Ninety-seven minutes, and the affection under the jokes is why they hold.

The dancers are the act; the man who brought them across the Atlantic is the problem. Mathieu Amalric puts the weight of Tournée on the one person who never performs - producer, driver, fixer, apologist - whose comeback depends entirely on performers whose work is not his. They supply the centre of gravity and most of the comedy. He supplies the desperation. Running 111 minutes in French, produced out of Germany, the picture takes the shape of a tour rather than a plot: arrivals, bookings negotiated, corridor arguments, the flat hours after a room empties. The distance between what he has promised and what he can actually arrange is where it finds its edge, and he is the last one to measure it.

The photography and the built world took two of the film's three Academy citations, which is a fair map of where its attention went. A young woman with no money and no protection falls in with a travelling carnival and meets a painter who owns nothing either; the story was old in 1927, and Frank Borzage is plainly not trying to renew it. He is trying to make it beautiful, which is a different and harder job. What the film does with light and constructed space is the argument, and the third citation, for the lead performance, is pitched to match - a role that has to carry destitution and appetite without a word of dialogue. 102 minutes. It asks for sentiment to be taken as a serious proposition, and the images are what make the request reasonable.

A young woman of the Southern gentry allows herself an interest in a man who works with his hands, and what she takes for amusement is, everywhere around her, a matter of property. Sam Taylor spends 76 minutes inside that mismatch: her freedom to play, set against a town where nobody else treats it as play. The class line is drawn early and drawn hard, and the drama comes of a woman finding that her own lightness acquires weight the moment it crosses. The Academy's Best Actress citation is why the title has survived at all, and the role explains the citation - written to be adored and blamed in the same breath, it needs a performer willing to let charm curdle into liability while the room is still enjoying it.

The land is sold, the livestock with it, and the passage that money buys covers two people. Haydar and Meryem have seven children. A grandfather's advice adds one boy to the party, and that amendment, offered as practical wisdom and accepted as hope, is the decision Xavier Koller never lets out of his sight. It begins in eastern Turkey with rumours of Swiss prosperity arriving as stories, which is exactly what the family is travelling on: not a job, not an address, a reputation other people's money has acquired at a distance. It won the Academy's award for international feature. At 110 minutes it stays patient with the ordinary business of leaving - the selling, the arranging, the goodbyes conducted as though they were temporary.
